stances.claim: Voting unanimously in Sara Z. Duterte v. House of Representatives (July 25 2025, per SAJ Marvic M.V.F. Leonen, en banc, 13-0 with Justice Caguioa inhibiting and Justice Singh on leave), the SC declared unconstitutional the articles of impeachment filed by the House against the VP for violating the one-year rule imposed by the Constitution. Accordingly, the Senate under then Senate President Francis 'Chiz' Escudero archived the Articles.
stances.rhetorical_move: case-citation opening + 13-0-en-banc-unanimous + one-year-rule violation + Senate-archiving sequence

stances.claim: By the same vote, the Court -- in a resolution dated Jan 29 2026 -- clarified that, in sum, after one year, impeachment complaints may be initiated anew in accordance with the Constitution and House rules. Significantly, the Court did not rule on the merits of the articles of impeachment. Consequently, four impeachment complaints were filed in the House. One was later withdrawn; another was dismissed; the two others -- 'filed by Fr. Joel Saballa et al.' and 'Atty. Nathaniel G. Cabrera' -- were declared sufficient in form and substance by the House committee on justice. Thereafter, the justice committee issued a 'Notice' directing the VP to file her 'Verified Answer' within a nonextendible 10 calendar days or until yesterday, March 15 2026.

At her option, the VP may or may not comply with the notice. However, her failure to file her Verified Answer within the said period 'shall be deemed a waiver of her right' to submit her answer and she 'shall be considered to have interposed a general denial.' Upon receipt of the answer, if any, the complainants were given three calendar days to file a reply, with a copy furnished to the VP. Upon receiving the reply, the VP may then file a rejoinder within three calendar days. During these exchanges, both parties may submit their supporting evidence, affidavits, and other pleadings.

After hearing and evaluating the evidence, the Justice Committee will determine -- by a vote of the majority of all its 40 regular members plus about 15 ex-officio -- whether probable cause exists. If majority is not obtained, the complaints would be deemed dismissed. If majority is obtained, the committee would submit a favorable report with appropriate articles of impeachment. If the report and Articles obtain the vote of at least one-third of the members of the House or 105 members, the Articles would be transmitted to the Senate for trial 'forthwith.' Note that the articles of impeachment thrown out by the Court on July 25 2025 were signed by 215 representatives.

These proceedings may make sense to lawyers, but to lay people, the question is -- how long will the process take before the supposed Articles will be transmitted to the Senate for trial 'forthwith'? The answer will depend partly on whether the Justice Committee could continue its proceedings during the congressional recess from March 21 to May 3 2026. Rep. Gerville Luistro, chair of the House Justice Committee, opined that because of the urgency expected by the people in expediting the proceedings, the committee can and should continue its hearings during the recess. With due respect, CJP believes the committee should refrain from so proceeding unless the House amends its rules or gives express authority. Should the committee proceed without such authority, it would be vulnerable to a petition in the SC to declare its proceedings unconstitutional -- in which case, if a TRO is issued by the Court or worse, judging them unconstitutional, the proceedings would be delayed indefinitely. However, as a caveat, the President may call a special session of Congress during the contemplated recess, in which case the committee could also proceed with its hearings.
stances.rhetorical_move: lay-people-question + Luistro-urgency-expedited opinion + CJP-with-due-respect-contrary-view + TRO-vulnerability + special-session-of-Congress caveat

stances.claim: There is no constitutional deadline limiting the length of the proceedings in the upper house, except that 'trial by the Senate shall forthwith proceed.' The trial of former President Joseph Estrada lasted roughly one month, because the prosecutors walked out after the Senate voted 12-11 to stop the opening of the 'second envelope' that was supposed to contain damning evidence against the then president. Instead, he was ousted by the Second People Power revolution. In contrast, the full trial of CJ Renato C. Corona spanned about five months. Given the foregoing, and assuming the complaints progress through the House and the articles of impeachment are transmitted to the Senate, the full trial could extend well into 2027, depending on scheduling, evidence presentation, legal challenges, and political dynamics.

As our people await accountability and clarity, we can take solace in Martin Luther King Jr.'s enduring insight: the arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice. True justice, in this context, demands thoroughness, not haste -- ensuring that any outcome rests on truth rather than on expediency.

notable_anecdotes: The Sara Z. Duterte v. House of Representatives 13-0 unanimous en banc vote (per SAJ Leonen) with two-justice non-participation (Caguioa inhibition + Singh leave) -- an unusually clean unanimous-on-merits result on a high-stakes political-case, removing any 'partisan split' framing.

The 215-representatives-signed original Articles thrown out -- captures the gap between political-momentum (215 = far above the 105 one-third threshold) and constitutional-procedural validity (one-year-rule violation).
The 'Fr. Joel Saballa et al.' first-surviving-complainant identification -- a priest-led complainant adding civic-religious dimension to the secular impeachment process.
The 'Atty. Nathaniel G. Cabrera' second-surviving-complainant -- a private-attorney lay-citizen complainant, demonstrating the broad-citizen access to impeachment-initiation.

The House Justice Committee 40-regular-plus-~15-ex-officio composition + voting-threshold -- a procedural-detail seldom captured precisely in mainstream coverage, but central to forecasting committee-stage outcomes.

The Joseph Estrada impeachment trial 'second envelope' 12-11 vote + prosecutors-walked-out + Second People Power ouster -- captures one of PH constitutional history's most consequential impeachment-aborted moments where extra-constitutional revolution finished what trial began.
The Renato C. Corona five-month full-trial baseline -- captures the only completed PH Senate impeachment trial as the duration-baseline for forecasting Sara-trial timeline.

The Rep. Gerville Luistro 'urgency expected by the people in expediting the proceedings' opinion -- captures the House-Justice-Chair's pro-continuation-during-recess position, which CJP gently contradicts.
The 'With due respect, I believe the committee should refrain' framing -- among CJP's most diplomatic procedural-prudence disagreements with a named active-officeholder.
The TRO-vulnerability + 'judging them unconstitutional' procedural-prudence warning -- CJP applying his SC-procedural-doctrine expertise to predict litigation-risks of committee-overreach.

The special-session-of-Congress presidential-discretion caveat -- CJP exhibiting his typical balanced-multi-track-procedural-knowledge by accommodating an alternative path he doesn't actively recommend but accurately catalogs.
The 'extend well into 2027' forward-projection -- captures CJP's calendar-anchored realistic-timeline estimate, distinguishing impatient-political-expectation from procedural-realism.

The Martin Luther King Jr. 'arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice' closing -- among CJP's most-cited closing-axioms across his column corpus, here applied specifically to the patience-justice-demands argument.
The 'demands thoroughness, not haste -- ensuring that any outcome rests on truth rather than on expediency' closing -- among CJP's tightest substance-over-speed impeachment-process formulations.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban traces the timeline of Vice President Sara Z. Duterte's impeachment process. Voting unanimously in Sara Z. Duterte v. House of Representatives (July 25 2025, per SAJ Marvic M.V.F. Leonen, en banc, 13-0 with Justice Caguioa inhibiting and Justice Singh on leave), the SC declared unconstitutional the articles of impeachment filed by the House against the VP for violating the one-year rule imposed by the Constitution. The Senate under then Senate President Francis 'Chiz' Escudero archived the Articles. By the same vote, the Court -- in a resolution dated Jan 29 2026 -- clarified that after one year, impeachment complaints may be initiated anew per the Constitution and House rules. Significantly, the Court did not rule on the merits of the articles of impeachment. Consequently, four impeachment complaints were filed in the House -- one withdrawn, another dismissed; the two others ('filed by Fr. Joel Saballa et al.' and 'Atty. Nathaniel G. Cabrera') declared sufficient in form and substance by the House committee on justice. The justice committee issued a 'Notice' directing the VP to file her Verified Answer within a nonextendible 10 calendar days, until yesterday, March 15 2026. At her option, the VP may or may not comply -- failure within the period 'shall be deemed a waiver' and she 'shall be considered to have interposed a general denial.' Upon receipt of the answer, complainants have three days to file a reply; the VP three days to file a rejoinder; both parties may submit supporting evidence, affidavits, and pleadings. The Justice Committee will determine -- by a vote of the majority of all its 40 regular members plus about 15 ex-officio -- whether probable cause exists. If majority is not obtained, the complaints are deemed dismissed. If obtained, the committee submits a favorable report with appropriate articles to the House; if the report and Articles obtain the vote of at least one-third of the members or 105, the Articles are transmitted to the Senate for trial 'forthwith.' Note that the articles thrown out by the Court on July 25 2025 were signed by 215 representatives. These proceedings may make sense to lawyers, but to lay people the question is: how long will the process take before the Articles are transmitted to the Senate for trial 'forthwith'? The answer depends partly on whether the Justice Committee could continue its proceedings during the March 21 to May 3 2026 congressional recess. Rep. Gerville Luistro, House Justice Committee chair, opined that because of the urgency expected by the people in expediting the proceedings, the committee can and should continue hearings during the recess. With due respect, CJP believes the committee should refrain unless the House amends its rules or gives express authority. Should the committee proceed without such authority, it would be vulnerable to a petition in the SC to declare its proceedings unconstitutional -- a TRO or unconstitutionality ruling would delay the proceedings indefinitely. As a caveat, the President may call a special session of Congress during the recess, in which case the committee could proceed. There is no constitutional deadline limiting the length of proceedings in the upper house, except that 'trial by the Senate shall forthwith proceed.' The trial of former President Joseph Estrada lasted roughly one month -- prosecutors walked out after the Senate voted 12-11 to stop the opening of the 'second envelope' supposed to contain damning evidence; instead Estrada was ousted by the Second People Power revolution. By contrast, the full trial of CJ Renato C. Corona spanned about five months. Assuming the complaints progress through the House and articles are transmitted to the Senate, the full trial could extend well into 2027, depending on scheduling, evidence presentation, legal challenges, and political dynamics. As our people await accountability and clarity, we can take solace in Martin Luther King Jr.'s enduring insight: the arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice. True justice, in this context, demands thoroughness, not haste -- ensuring that any outcome rests on truth rather than on expediency.
